title: The Black Death (1348)
hook: Jews are blamed for the plague and whole communities murdered

segments.voice: Yesterday, expelled: a street in London that still remembers. Your line was pushed out, with a deadline. Did you find a place name with a story? Today, a sickness, and the blame that followed it. Day nine hundred forty.

A sickness moves along the trade routes into Europe. It arrives in a town, and within days families are burying their own. Nobody understands how it spreads. Doctors argue about bad air and the stars. Priests call for prayer and processions. And in town after town, a rumor arrives as well, sometimes before the sickness itself: the Jews are poisoning the wells. Today, the Black Death, and what fear did with that rumor.
screen: `A SICKNESS ON THE TRADE ROUTES.` → `NOBODY KNOWS HOW IT SPREADS.` → `A RUMOR ARRIVES TOO.`

segments.voice: The plague killed rich and poor, Christian and Jew. But the rumor needed someone to blame. In some places, Jews were arrested and tortured until they confessed to poisoning, and those forced confessions were copied and sent on to other towns as proof. And the killing spread. In parts of the German lands, in Switzerland, in Alsace, whole communities were murdered, often burned, sometimes before the plague had even reached the town. Some voices pushed back. Pope Clement the Sixth issued a bull that answered the rumor directly. He pointed out that Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else, and that it was raging in places where no Jews lived at all. He ordered that Jews not be harmed. In town after town, the killing went on anyway. Our line today borrows a word from the Day of Atonement, though the Torah means something very different by it. In Leviticus the high priest takes two goats. One is offered. Over the other he lays his hands and confesses the sins of the people, and then the goat is sent off into the wilderness. The Hebrew says it goes to Azazel. The King James Bible gives the English word, saying the goat is kept alive "to let him go for a scapegoat into the wilderness." Notice what the ritual does. The priest names the people's own wrongs, out loud, before the goat goes. At the center of the rite is taking responsibility. The plague years ran it backward: a frightened crowd invented guilt and laid it on the people next door. The goat carried away sins the people had confessed as their own. The Jews of those towns were blamed for sins nobody had committed.
screen: `A RUMOR NEEDS SOMEONE TO BLAME.` · `CLEMENT THE SIXTH ANSWERS IT.` · `TWO GOATS ON THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE NAME THEIR OWN SINS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: refuse to scapegoat anyone. Let your shoulders drop and your breath slow. Think of something going wrong right now: at work, at home, in the news. Notice if your mind has already chosen someone to blame, especially someone who isn't in the room. Gently set that name down. Ask instead: what part of this is simply hard, and what part is mine? Rest with that question. The bell holds the time.
Azazel. Where the Torah's scapegoat is sent in Leviticus, the image behind a plague-year rumor that blamed Jews for the Black Death. Today's word.
Your line: no scapegoats. Today, when something goes wrong and a name comes to mind, check whether it's the cause or just the easiest target. Day nine hundred forty.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, Jews read the Torah's account of the two goats in the synagogue service and confess their own wrongs aloud, together, in the first person plural.

fork.setup: you are Pope Clement the Sixth. reports arrive that Jews are being killed as poisoners. what do you write?
options: that the Jews must be investigated first.
nothing; it is a local matter.

fork.reveal: he issued a bull saying exactly that, though in town after town the killing went on.

original.note: Hebrew: Azazel, where the second goat is sent in Leviticus 16; what the name means is debated.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scapegoat is just someone who gets unfairly blamed.
what it means: in Leviticus a goat is sent into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement, after the high priest confesses the people's own sins over it.
what a scholar hears: during the Black Death the pattern ran in reverse, and Clement the Sixth's bull rebutted the poisoning charge.

notes: Editor: removed the year 1348 from the voice (it stays only in the index title); the teach said 'there is a word for what happened' but never named it, so it now names the scapegoat with the KJV wording of Leviticus 16:10 beside the Hebrew Azazel; cut the line attributing a motive ('its own helplessness') to the crowds.
Regions named (German lands, Switzerland, Alsace) and the forced confessions being circulated: please check against standard histories.
Clement VI's arguments (Jews dying too; plague where no Jews lived) are paraphrased; please confirm wording.
The reading of the Leviticus 16 ritual as beginning with confession of the people's own sins is a description of 16:21; please confirm framing.
'In town after town, the killing went on anyway' is a general statement; soften if needed.
Azazel spelling and pronunciation: please confirm.

Auditor: 'Then the killing began' implied all killings followed the forced confessions (some, e.g. in Provence, came earlier), now 'the killing spread'; 'the ritual begins with confession' was inexact (Leviticus 16 begins with the priest's own offering; the confession is 16:21), reworded; garbled closing lines ('The goat was sent away. These were neighbors.') rewritten.
